tldr: The authors propose "2AM," a framework that fully concentrates long-horizon task memory into a high-level Agent while guiding an RGB-only low-level Action Model using language and 2D prompt hints (grasp, place, move). On the LIBERO-Mem benchmark, without depth sensors or geometric planners, it achieved a 76.3% completion rate, significantly outperforming previously reported baselines.
hero_caption: Overview of the 2AM system. An Agent (VLM) that maintains and reasons over task history is loosely coupled with an Action Model (VLA) that holds no history and executes only local motions from RGB observations, connected via a steerable interface consisting of language and 2D pixel coordinates.
overview:
To perform long-horizon manipulation requiring multiple sequential steps, robots need "memory" of what they have done in the past. However, trying to embed this memory directly inside the low-level control policy (VLA) often causes it to get dragged down by failed past trajectories, making recovery difficult. Conversely, relying heavily on external planners or geometric tools with depth sensors muddles the attribution of improvements—is the gain due to richer sensors or the actual capability of the policy?

To address this, the authors designed a clean separation of roles: keep all memory in the high-level Agent, and restrict the low-level Action Model to stateless RGB-based control without episodic history. The key lies in the interface connecting the two. The Agent compiles its intentions from past history into not just text instructions, but 2D hints on the RGB image: grasp, place, and move coordinates. The Action Model autonomously handles approach, contact, and trajectory generation, while the Agent reassesses the scene and updates instructions at every short action chunk.

The authors evaluated this setup on the long-horizon benchmark "LIBERO-Mem." Under a pure RGB setup without depth information or additional planners, 2AM achieved an average completion rate of 76.3%. This surpasses a strong $\pi_0$ baseline re-implemented under the same setup (70.8%) and shows a dramatic 25.6-point improvement in relaxed success rate from 37.4% to 63.0%. By offloading contextual memory outside the action model and guiding it via grounded prompt hints, the framework brings out the policy's general-purpose motor capabilities to the fullest.
contributions: Proposed a loosely coupled architecture that fully isolates task history memory into a high-level Agent, constraining the low-level Action Model to a single RGB model with no episodic history.
Designed a compositional interface translating memory-grounded physical intent into subtask language and three types of 2D prompt hints (grasp, place, move) across different time scales.

Established an offline training recipe that extracts steering labels from demonstrations without teacher models, training with condition dropout, spatial noise, and temporal jitter to tolerate imperfect Agent outputs.

sections.heading: Dividing Memory and Control: Why Should We Expand Interface Bandwidth?
sections.summary: This section poses the fundamental question of whether memory in long-horizon manipulation belongs inside the control policy or with an external agent. The paper deliberately constrains tools and sensors, resolving the challenge by thickening the communication interface between the Agent and the Action Model.
sections.details:
Achieving general-purpose physical intelligence requires more than just extending action prediction horizons; a robot must remember task progress and translate that memory into appropriate physical motions. Modern Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel at short-term motor skills, while Vision-Language Model (VLM) agents excel at long-horizon reasoning and context tracking. However, when combining the two, the boundary of responsibilities has remained ambiguous.

A common remedy is to add recurrent connections or image histories inside the VLA. Yet, policies trained on demonstration data with history often latch onto failed trajectories and cannot recover. On the other hand, equipping external agents with a broad suite of tools, such as planners and 3D depth sensors, makes it hard to identify what drove success—did the sensors help, or did the tools simply compensate for an under-specified language interface?

The authors instead propose "2AM," a design philosophy that restricts sensors strictly to RGB cameras and narrows tool breadth, while expanding the "bandwidth" of the interface connecting the Agent and Action Model. All memory resides in the high-level Agent, keeping the low-level Action Model completely stateless regarding episodic history. The Agent issues subtask language and 2D grasp, place, and move hints based on history, and the Action Model uses them as guideposts to generate trajectories autonomously.

captions.F1: Overall view of the agent-side memory and steering interface. The Agent summarizes interaction history to decide the next intent, generating subtask language and 2D prompt hints. The Action Model receives no past history and executes short-horizon action chunks solely from current RGB images, robot states, and prompt hints.

sections.heading: The Rules of the "Steering Contract" Binding Agent and Action Model
sections.summary: This section defines a clear contract between the Agent and the Action Model. The Action Model holds no episodic history, operating solely on current RGB observations, robot states, and the language and multi-timescale 2D hints provided by the Agent.
sections.details:
At the core of 2AM lies a clear division of roles (contract): the Agent handles memory and reasoning, while the Action Model focuses purely on physical execution.

### 2.1 Problem Formulation: Separating Task State from Local Control State
Long-horizon object manipulation mixes fast local control states, such as current contact and gripper opening, with slow task states, such as object identity and repetition counts. 2AM hypothesizes that as long as the current RGB image is available, the influence of slow task states can be communicated to local motions via a compact steering command $c_k$, allowing the Action Model to remain conditionally independent of the full history $H_k$. Depth sensors, 3D geometric models, and predefined grasping scripts are entirely omitted.

### 2.2 Model Separation and Execution Cycle
The Agent retains summarized history $H_k$ and generates a steering command $c_k$ from the current RGB image $I^a_k$. In contrast, the Action Model has no access to $H_k$; taking only the current camera images, robot state, and $c_k$ as input, it predicts an absolute end-effector action chunk of length $L$. The Agent operates in a closed loop, re-observing the scene and updating instructions at each short action chunk.

### 2.3 Compositional Steering Interface Design
The steering command consists of a local language instruction $\ell_k$ and up to three 2D hint points normalized to $[0, 1000]^2$:
- Grasp point ($q^{\mathrm{grasp}}$): A short-term hint uniquely specifying the target instance before contact. It disappears from the view once grasped, preventing regression back to old coordinates.
- Place point ($q^{\mathrm{place}}$): A long-term hint indicating the target location during transit. It retains the overall goal even if lost from the wrist camera or occluded by the arm.
- Move point ($q^{\mathrm{move}}$): A medium-term directional hint pointing to the gripper position several steps ahead. It acts not as a strict waypoint, but as a vector showing the rough direction of movement.

None of these hints are strictly required; they are independently provided or omitted depending on the current task phase. The Action Model references them while autonomously deciding obstacle avoidance and contact timing.

sections.heading: Training from Demos without Teacher Models: Robustness Against Imperfect Guidance
sections.summary: A pipeline was developed to automatically extract training data for the Action Model from offline demonstrations. The model is trained with condition dropout and spatial noise to endure Agent mispredictions, omissions, and timing delays during inference.
sections.details:
When training a steerable action model, having a VLM annotate demonstration videos with ground-truth instructions step-by-step is expensive and unstable. 2AM deterministically and geometrically recovers ground-truth labels directly from offline robot demonstrations.

### 3.1 Teacher-Free Ground-Truth Label Extraction
Hint points are derived from object bounding boxes, contact sensors, and end-effector positions present in the demonstration trajectories. Grasp and place points are assigned as the normalized center coordinates of the target object's bounding box. Because these are merely "semantic centers" rather than geometrically optimal contact points, fine-tuning the actual grasp pose is left to the Action Model's own visual feedback. For the move point, a time window $[t+k_{\min}, t+k_{\max}]$ is randomly sampled from actual future end-effector coordinates, allowing the model to absorb temporal jitter caused by Agent inference latency.

### 3.2 Perturbations and Dropout to Tolerate Imperfect Steering
During deployment, the Agent might omit hints, drift by several pixels, or lag in updating instructions. Training exclusively on pristine guidance causes interface brittleness; thus, three training perturbations are applied:
- Condition dropout: Language, grasp, place, and move fields are independently masked at random (constrained so that not all conditions are dropped simultaneously). This enables execution with language only, points only, or partial hints.
- Spatial coordinate noise: Isotropic Gaussian noise is added to remaining 2D coordinates.
- Temporal sampling window: A randomized temporal span is applied to move point references.

The model utilizes Qwen3-VL-4B as the backbone, predicting 16-step action chunks via a Flow-matching Action Expert.

captions.F2: Training pipeline from offline demonstrations. Ground-truth guidance is extracted from demonstration object data and end-effector trajectories. After applying condition dropout, spatial noise, and temporal jitter perturbations, a single Flow-matching Action Model (Qwen3-VL-4B + Action Expert) is trained.

sections.heading: Evaluation on LIBERO-Mem: The Grounding Power of 2D Hints
sections.summary: Evaluation was conducted on the challenging memory benchmark "LIBERO-Mem." 2AM achieved an average completion rate of 76.3%, demonstrating a ~22.6-point improvement in completion rate and a ~43.6-point gain in relaxed success over language-only guidance.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Benchmark Setup and Evaluation Metrics
Evaluation was performed on "LIBERO-Mem" (10 tasks in total), where the robot performs repeated pick-and-place routines while altering target objects, destinations, and repetition counts based on past history. Comparisons were made against $\pi_0$ and SlotSSM as reported in the original benchmark paper, alongside a strong reproduced $\pi_0$ baseline built by the authors using the exact same Qwen3-VL-4B backbone as 2AM. Metrics include "Strict Success" (stopping precisely at the specified count), "Relaxed Success" (reaching the target state at least once), and "Completion Rate" (subgoal progress).

### 4.2 Experimental Results and Ablations
The reproduced $\pi_0$ baseline was far stronger than the original paper's reported 5.0%, achieving a 70.79% completion rate. Compared to this strong baseline, 2AM increased the completion rate to 76.29% (+5.50 points) and achieved a dramatic 25.58-point gain in Relaxed Success, jumping from 37.42% to 63.00%. Strict Success remained comparable at 11.83% (versus 12.25% for $\pi_0$).

To verify interface efficacy, an ablation omitting all 2D hints and providing only language subtasks (Language-only) was conducted. Here, Relaxed Success plunged to 19.42% and the completion rate dropped to 53.72%. Adding prompt hints resulted in a 43.58-point leap in Relaxed Success, proving that 2D hints play a decisive role in driving task progress.

Task-level breakdowns show 2AM's pronounced superiority in complex tasks involving relational reasoning and occlusions (T7–T10). However, the persistent gap between Relaxed (63.0%) and Strict (11.8%) highlights that even when the Agent completes tasks in the correct order, determining precisely when to stop after the exact number of repetitions remains a significant bottleneck.

captions.F3: Representative Agent guidance errors observed during evaluation. Left: local spatial offset in grasp location; Middle: incorrect subtask selection; Right: misidentified target placement basket. Training-time robustification mitigates minor coordinate offsets, but cannot fully compensate for high-level semantic mis-selections.

sections.heading: Boundaries with Related Work: How Does It Differ from Prior Systems?
sections.summary: This section reviews existing agentic robot systems and memory approaches to clarify 2AM's uniqueness. It decisively distinguishes itself by providing multi-faceted, image-grounded prompt hints to a single RGB action model without relying on external geometric tools or text-only interfaces.
sections.details:
### Comparison with Agentic VLA Systems
Recent systems (such as Hi Robot, Goal2Skill, CodeGraphVLP, and Harness VLA) augment VLAs with planners, 3D value maps, and self-recovery loops to enhance system capability. However, alternative motor scripts and privileged geometric data obscure the true drivers of success. 2AM deliberately discards alternative tools to examine how much can be solved purely through the contractual relationship between a single action model and an agent.

### Interfaces Bridging Reasoning and Control
The value of intermediate representations has been highlighted by works such as RT-H's language motions, HAMSTER's 2D paths, and Steerable Policies' various prompt formats. 2AM advances this by injecting the physical consequence of the Agent's long-term memory into the Action Model via a compact, compositional interface of three multi-timescale 2D hints (grasp, place, move).

### Where to Place Memory
Contrasting with methods embedding recurrent states inside the VLA (such as MemoryVLA and SlotSSM), frameworks like MemER and PrediMem externalize memory to a higher-level agent. However, systems like MemER communicated with low-level policies solely through text. 2AM shares this externalized memory philosophy but augments under-specified text with grounded 2D hints to convey physical intent.

sections.heading: Uncovered Challenges and Future Horizons
sections.summary: Limitations include confinement to simulation and the inability of 2D hints to represent contact force or complete occlusions. The trade-offs surrounding strict termination criteria and inference latency are also discussed.
sections.details:
While the results offer valuable insights, clear limitations remain:

- Benchmark scope: Verification is limited to simulated LIBERO-Mem, assuming tasks where intent can be grounded onto RGB images. The 2D interface cannot handle tasks requiring geometry of completely hidden objects, delicate contact force feedback, or continuous motion history.
- Termination difficulty: Despite high completion (76.3%) and relaxed success (63.0%), strict success (stopping at the specified count) remains low at 11.8%, showing that precise termination recognition on the Agent side remains an unresolved bottleneck.
- Fine-grained ablation: The individual contributions of each of the three hint types (grasp, place, move), agent scaling (currently using Qwen3.8-27B), and the trade-off between update frequency and latency have not been fully isolated.

The authors plan to expand evaluation to diverse memory benchmarks such as RMBench and RoboMME, alongside real-robot closed-loop verification using pure RGB inputs without privileged data.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A Policy's True Worth Depends on the Agent's Steering Precision
sections.summary: This section synthesizes the effectiveness of keeping task memory on the Agent side while guiding a stateless Action Model with grounded hints. Action Model execution depends not only on what the policy has learned, but on how precisely the high-level Agent can steer its physical intent.
sections.details:
Under the clear division of "Agent remembers, Action Model acts," 2AM introduced a compositional steering interface combining language with 2D prompt hints. In-depth experiments on LIBERO-Mem demonstrated that hint-guided steering dramatically advances task progress.

The most critical takeaway from this work is that the true capability of an Action Model (VLA) depends not merely on what the policy has learned, but on how precisely the Agent can steer it. Rather than evaluating VLA capabilities through ambiguous language instructions alone, this work demonstrates the importance of communicating physical intention through a well-grounded interface with adequate bandwidth.

takeaways: Instead of forcing long-term task memory into a low-level action policy (VLA), centralizing it inside a high-level VLM agent preserves policy statelessness and improves recovery.
Pairing language with 2D image coordinates (grasp, place, move) substantially widens the interface bandwidth for conveying physical intent to the Action Model.
Training the Action Model with condition dropout, spatial noise, and temporal jitter makes it highly resilient to Agent reasoning mistakes and coordinate inaccuracies.
Making correct task progress and cleanly halting at an exact repetition count are distinct challenges; the latter demands dedicated termination mechanisms.
limitations: Because guidance relies on 2D image prompts, the framework struggles with tasks involving visually hidden objects or requiring force feedback.
A wide gap persists between task progress (Relaxed Success: 63.0%) and strict termination (Strict Success: 11.8%), indicating semantic stopping criteria remain challenging.
Evaluations are restricted to simulated environments (LIBERO-Mem); real-robot performance subject to inference latency and sensor noise has not been tested.
